final_answer:
Short answer: probably not as a categorical matter, but it depends on facts the hypothetical leaves open; the dispersal order and arrests are lawful only if they rest on something more than the protest's content or generalized concern, and on the stated facts that showing is doubtful. Caveat: most primary texts could not be opened (several research sites were blocked), so the points below rest on search-result summaries and my background knowledge, and should be cite-checked.

1. Framework. Peaceful assembly and protest on public sidewalks and plazas is core First Amendment activity (Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963): convictions of about 187 peaceful demonstrators who refused a police dispersal order, for breach of the peace, were reversed; the State may not criminalize peaceful expression of unpopular views). Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965), likewise bars using breach-of-peace laws against peaceable demonstrations merely because onlookers might react. Police concern about 'potential escalation' alone, with no imminent violence, is thus not enough under these cases. A heckler's veto is not a valid basis.

2. Government may nonetheless regulate time, place and manner. Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972), upholds content-neutral regulation, and the question is whether the manner of expression is basically incompatible with the normal activity of the place at that time. Demonstrators who spill into and block a street, creating real traffic disruption or safety danger, are not protected in doing so, and police may order them back to the sidewalk. Here the facts say people only 'occasionally stepped into the street' while mostly staying on the sidewalk, which is weak support for dispersing the whole assembly, though a narrower order (stay out of the roadway) would be easier to justify. Verbal arguments with passers-by are generally protected absent fighting words or true threats.

3. Illinois/Chicago law supplying the arrest basis. Under Chicago Municipal Code 8-4-010(d) (as reported in secondary summaries; I could not open the text), failure to obey a lawful dispersal order is an offense only where the officer is identifiable and three or more persons in the immediate vicinity are committing disorderly conduct likely to cause substantial harm. Illinois mob action, 720 ILCS 5/25-1, penalizes a participant in a mob action who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer (Class A misdemeanor, per secondary summary), but mob action requires force or violence, or an assembly with intent to commit an offense or do violence. A peaceful protest with signs and chanting does not fit those predicates. If the predicate disorderly conduct is absent, the dispersal order is unlawful as applied and arrests for disobeying it lack probable cause under state law; a Fourth Amendment/false arrest claim and an as-applied First Amendment claim would then be strong. In Schirmer v. Nagode, 621 F.3d 581 (7th Cir. 2010), the Seventh Circuit vacated an injunction against 8-4-010(d) on standing grounds, so the provision's facial validity was left undecided.

4. Seventh Circuit precedent on mass dispersal arrests. Vodak v. City of Chicago, 639 F.3d 738 (7th Cir. 2011), arising from the 2003 Iraq-war march, treated whether police had probable cause for mass arrests as turning on disputed facts: whether an order to disperse was effectively communicated, whether the crowd was peaceable, and whether a particular arrestee was given a chance to leave. Arrests of persons not given a dispersal order or an opportunity to comply are problematic. Note also that Vodak resolved the case largely on probable cause and qualified immunity/liability grounds rather than announcing a bright-line First Amendment rule, so individual officers may still obtain qualified immunity where the law was not clearly established, and the City is liable only through Monell (policy or custom).

5. Application. On the stated facts (peaceful, mostly on sidewalk, signs and chanting, only verbal arguments, police citing traffic concerns and potential escalation), the order looks vulnerable: Edwards and Cox disfavor dispersal based on speculation, and the local ordinance requires actual disorderly conduct by three or more people likely to cause substantial harm. The City's best arguments are (a) repeated street blockage creating real traffic or safety hazards, (b) acts that amount to disorderly conduct, and (c) a narrow, content-neutral, clearly communicated order with adequate time to comply and an alternative place to remain. Whether each of the 30 arrestees personally obstructed traffic or was warned also matters. Because Illinois law and probable cause are the proximate issues, claims will likely be framed as First Amendment retaliation/as-applied, Fourth Amendment unlawful arrest (probable cause is generally a defense to retaliatory arrest claims under Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391 (2019), not independently researched here), and challenges to the ordinance.

6. Bottom line. Ordering dispersal of a truly peaceful protest on speculation about escalation likely violates the First Amendment (and arrests under it would lack probable cause); but the answer would change if evidence shows substantial obstruction of the roadway, violence or imminent threats, or if the order was narrowly tailored and clearly communicated. Date: answered as of October 2, 2025 facts; no later authority was checked beyond the sources listed, and no authority specific to July 2025 events was located.

authorities.title: Edwards v. South Carolina
authorities.proposition: Convictions of peaceful demonstrators who refused a police dispersal order, under a breach-of-peace theory, violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments absent violence or threat.

authorities.title: Cox v. Louisiana
authorities.proposition: Breach-of-peace laws cannot be applied to punish peaceable demonstrations because they might provoke violence by others.

authorities.citation: Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972)
authorities.title: Grayned v. City of Rockford
authorities.proposition: Reasonable content-neutral time, place and manner regulations are permitted; test is whether manner of expression is basically incompatible with the normal activity of the place at that time.

authorities.title: Vodak v. City of Chicago

claims.text: Dispersing a peaceful assembly based on speculative escalation or onlooker reaction is not permitted under Edwards and Cox.
Content-neutral regulation, including ordering demonstrators out of the roadway, is permitted under time/place/manner doctrine, so real street obstruction is a legitimate basis.
The Chicago failure-to-disperse offense and Illinois mob action require predicate disorderly conduct/violence; absent them an arrest lacks probable cause.
Seventh Circuit treats probable cause for mass dispersal arrests as fact-dependent on notice, opportunity to comply, and peaceable character; 8-4-010(d) facial validity remains undecided.
Defenses and remedies: qualified immunity, Monell, and the Nieves probable-cause rule may limit recovery (Nieves not independently researched).
On the stated facts the order is vulnerable, but outcome depends on extent of street obstruction, notice, and tailoring.
